sections.title_en: The Mitzva 'You Shall Not Stand by the Blood of Your Fellow'
sections.body_en:
It is a great Torah mitzva to save a person who is in danger. For we are commanded even to return to a person an object he lost, as it is said (Devarim 22:2): "and you shall return it to him"; all the more so we must return to him his life and save him. And likewise the mitzva is learned from the verse (Vayikra 19:16): "You shall not stand by the blood of your fellow", and so the Sages said (Sanhedrin 73a): From where do we learn that one who sees his fellow drowning in a river, or a wild beast dragging him and about to tear him apart, or bandits coming upon him to kill him, is obligated to save him? The Torah teaches: "You shall not stand by the blood of your fellow."

That is, in addition to the basic mitzva "and you shall love your fellow as yourself" (Vayikra 19:18), about which Rabbi Akiva said that it is a great principle of the Torah, and which of course includes within it all the good relations that should prevail between a person and his fellow, the Torah spelled out a further command: "You shall not stand by the blood of your fellow." It is not enough to smile at one's fellow and sometimes even to help him; rather the Torah establishes that a person has responsibility and is a guarantor towards his fellow. If his fellow is in trouble, he is obligated to rise to his help, and not to spare effort and money in saving his fellow.

And likewise regarding obstacles in the public domain that may cause harm to passers-by, there is a mitzva to remove them because of "You shall not stand by the blood of your fellow". And likewise one who sees an obstacle on the road that may cause risk to travellers is obligated to see to its removal, by notifying the police, or by his own efforts when he can remove it without endangering himself.

If we conduct ourselves so, and feel in our hearts the mutual responsibility among all Israel, we will be able to establish a consolidated and united society, which will be able to cope with the great challenges from within and without, and to realise the great vision of the people of Israel.

One of the mitzvot that teach the magnitude of public responsibility for human life is the mitzva of the beheaded heifer (egla arufa). As it is said (Devarim 21:1-2): "If one be found slain in the land which the Lord your God gives you to possess, lying in the field, and it is not known who struck him, then your elders and your judges shall go out, and they shall measure to the cities that are round about the slain." That is, the responsibility to remove dangers from people rests on the whole public and its leaders. And when they did not succeed in preventing bloodshed, a public reckoning of the soul must be made. Therefore the great ones of the generation go out to examine what happened, and which city is near to the slain man, on which rests an indirect responsibility for the murder that took place in its vicinity. Through the public occupation with the murder of the slain man, the whole community will internalise the terrible severity of murder. It may be that through this, in the end, the person will be found who will expose the murderer, and they will be able to punish him (Rambam, Guide 3:40).

After it was clarified which city is nearest, the elders of that city and its judges, together with the kohanim, would bring a heifer and break its neck beside the stream. "And all the elders of that city who are nearest to the slain man shall wash their hands over the heifer whose neck was broken in the stream. And they shall answer and say: Our hands have not shed this blood, neither have our eyes seen it" (ibid. 6-7). Their words are shocking: is it conceivable that the elders of that city shed the blood of the slain man?! The Sages explain (Sota 45b): "Rather, he did not come into our hands and we sent him away without food, and we did not see him and leave him without escort." That is, in a matter as severe as murder, even very indirect responsibility has significance.

Perhaps that murdered man did not know his way, and erred and fell into the hands of bandits, and had they escorted him he would have gone on the king's highway and lived. And also, if the traveller was hungry and they did not give him food, responsibility rests on the people of the city and their leaders. Perhaps he will die of hunger, and perhaps because of his hunger he will rob people and kill or be killed. That is, even consent to there being people hungry for bread carries a certain responsibility for murder.

To our sorrow, we hear of people who are murdered at the entrance of a shop or in a quarrel over parking, and the leaders of the public are not shocked by the murder as they should be. According to the guidance of the Torah, immediately upon the news of the murder becoming known, an important meeting should have been convened, headed by a minister, the mayor, the local rabbi and the local police commander, with the participation of senior representatives of the ministries of education, welfare, justice and internal security, in order to make a reckoning of the soul. Perhaps they did not relate to the problems when they began to arise? Perhaps they ignored minor offences and opened the gate to severe crimes? Perhaps the punishment is not sufficiently deterrent? Perhaps the education system is not fulfilling its duty?

Only afterwards will it be possible to ask: "Forgive Your people Israel, whom You have redeemed, O Lord, and do not lay innocent blood in the midst of Your people Israel; and the blood shall be forgiven them" (ibid. 8).

A person who sees that an injustice is being done to his fellow must protest against the doers of the injustice, and there are two mitzvot in this. The first is to save the oppressed from the hand of his oppressor, and this too is included in the mitzva "You shall not stand by the blood of your fellow". The second is to rebuke the sinner, in order to prevent him from sinning, or at least to express protest against the evil deed. Rebuke of sin does not stem from hatred; on the contrary, it stems from love and responsibility towards each one of Israel: just as there is a mitzva to save one's fellow from monetary harm, so there is a mitzva to save his soul from sin. And this is what is said (Vayikra 19:17-18): "You shall not hate your brother in your heart; you shall surely rebuke your fellow, and not bear sin because of him… and you shall love your fellow as yourself; I am the Lord."

One who could have protested and did not protest is considered as though he committed that sin. And as the Sages said (Shabbat 54b): "Whoever can protest against the members of his household and does not protest is held responsible for the members of his household; against the people of his city, he is held responsible for the people of his city; against the whole world, he is held responsible for the whole world."

Especially obligated in this is one who is connected to people of authority and government, on whom it rests to rebuke them when they behave wickedly and abuse those weaker than them. And so Rav Papa said about those close to the 'Resh Galuta' (the Exilarch), that they are held responsible for the sins of the Resh Galuta and the members of his household. The Resh Galuta was the head of the Jews of the Diaspora, whose centre was in Babylonia. Great governmental power was given into his hand by the Persian government; it was in the power of the Resh Galuta and his men to appoint people to senior positions or dismiss them, to grant trading rights or withdraw them, and to divide the burden of tax as he understood. Therefore Rav Papa said that the members of the household of the Resh Galuta are held responsible for the sin of the whole world, because they have the power to protest against the sinners (Shabbat 54b).

When people of government behave improperly, their sin is very great, because the public learns from their ways and is drawn after them for the bad. In addition, since they have great power, their harm is severe: they oppress and rob, pervert judgement, weave conspiracies, in order to amass for themselves great wealth and honour. And so it is told in the Talmud (Shabbat 55a) that Rabbi Zeira said to Rabbi Simon: you must rebuke the members of the household of the Resh Galuta for their evil deeds. Apparently Rabbi Simon had connections with them, and therefore Rabbi Zeira demanded of Rabbi Simon to rebuke them. Rabbi Simon answered him: they do not accept my rebuke, so why should I rebuke them for nothing? It is of course fitting to add that people of government hate rebuke, and one who rebukes them may pay a personal price for it. Therefore Rabbi Simon held that if in any case they will not accept his rebuke, there is no point in rebuking them.

Rabbi Zeira answered him: even though they will not accept, you are obligated to rebuke them, as Rabbi Aḥa son of Rabbi Ḥanina said: "Never did a good measure go out from the mouth of the Holy One, blessed be He, and He retracted it for evil, except for this matter." That is, after a good instruction goes out from Heaven, the Holy One, blessed be He, does not retract it, except in a case concerning people who could have rebuked the sinners and did not rebuke. As it was when God decreed the destruction of the Temple: at first He decreed to punish the wicked alone, and then He decreed again to punish the righteous for not having protested. And this is what is said (Yeḥezkel 9:4): "And the Lord said to him: Go through the midst of the city, through the midst of Jerusalem, and set a mark upon the foreheads of the men who sigh and cry for all the abominations that are done in its midst," etc.

The Sages explained that at first the Holy One, blessed be He, said to Gavriel: Go and write on the foreheads of the righteous a tav (sign) of ink, so that the angels of destruction will not have power over them; and on the foreheads of the wicked a tav of blood, so that the angels of destruction will have power over them. The Attribute of Justice said before the Holy One, blessed be He: Master of the world, how are these different from those? He said to it: These are completely righteous, and those are completely wicked. It said before Him: Master of the world, it was in their (these righteous ones') power to protest and they did not protest! He said to it: It is revealed and known before Me that had they protested against them, they would not have accepted from them. It said before Him: Master of the world, if it is revealed before You, to them who revealed it?! And this is what is written (ibid. 9:6): "Slay utterly old and young, maidens and little children and women… and begin at My sanctuary." And it is written (there): "Then they began with the elders who were before the house." And Rav Yosef explained that these elders, with whom the calamity began, were "people who kept the whole Torah from alef to tav", and only the mitzva of protest they did not keep, and for this they were punished first.

When Avraham our father heard from the Holy One, blessed be He, that a decree of destruction had been decreed upon Sedom and Amora, he stood and prayed for them, and argued that if there is in Sedom a good core of righteous people who are ready to struggle for their position, there is a chance that in the end the righteous will prevail over the wicked and bring the inhabitants of the city back in repentance, and so the complete repair will come to Sedom and Amora without the need to destroy it. But after it became clear to him that there were not even ten righteous people there, he did not continue to plead for them any more (Bereshit 18).

And one should note precisely the words of Avraham our father, who argued (ibid. 24): "Perhaps there are fifty righteous within the city; will You indeed sweep away and not forgive the place for the sake of the fifty righteous who are in its midst?" And so God answered him (ibid. 26): "And the Lord said: If I find in Sedom fifty righteous within the city, then I will forgive the whole place for their sake." Rav Avraham Ibn Ezra explained: "And the reason for 'within the city': that they fear God in public", for then there is a chance that they will prevail over the wickedness. But if they live their private "righteous" lives inside their homes, there is no chance that they will repair the public. And to some extent their influence may be the opposite: if they live beside the sinning public and do not protest, it follows that they strengthen its hands to some extent. For the wicked will say to themselves: here, these righteous people sit beside us and say nothing to us, which implies that our deeds are acceptable.

It follows, then, according to the Ibn Ezra, that there may have been in Sedom ten private righteous people who did not take part in their wicked deeds, but they shut themselves inside their homes and did not protest. They saw how orphans and the poor were tormented, and were silent. They heard the cry of that righteous and wretched girl who gave food to a poor man and was cruelly killed, and they kept still. And therefore they too were punished with the wicked.

And only Lot was saved, in the merit of his closeness to Avraham: when guests came to him he took them in, as he had learned from Avraham our father, and when the people of Sedom sought to torment them he stood and saved them, as he had learned from Avraham our father. And there was in this some protest against their deeds, and in this merit he was saved.

The Ibn Ezra added and explained that in the days of the destruction of the First Temple too there were in Jerusalem private righteous people who did not protest against the wicked, and therefore Jerusalem was not saved for their sake; and this is what is said (Yirmeyahu 5:1): "Run to and fro through the streets of Jerusalem, and see now and know, and seek in its broad places, if you can find a man, if there is any who does justice, who seeks faithfulness, and I will pardon her." But there was not in the streets and the broad places a man who seeks faithfulness and does justice, and therefore Jerusalem was destroyed.

Heroic righteous people who are not ashamed to fight for their positions and to fight wickedness have great power to plead in defence before the Holy One, blessed be He. For they cannot be suspected of giving up truth and justice out of weakness; on the contrary, their whole lives are dedicated to revealing the divine good in the world, and therefore when they plead in defence their words are accepted.1

notes_en.en: See the wonderful words of Rav Soloveitchik in the essay 'Kol Dodi Dofek' p. 72. On the basis of the Gemara, Bava Batra 15b, which brought differing views on when Iyov lived, or whether he was only a parable, he explained the meaning of Iyov's sufferings: although he was blameless and upright, and also helped the poor who turned to him, nevertheless he did not bear the burden of the public and did not truly share in the pain and suffering of others. And this is the claim, as it were, that the Holy One, blessed be He, claimed against him: "You were a contemporary of Yaakov, who struggled with Lavan, Esav and the man at the stream of Yabbok; did you help him with counsel and resourcefulness? Who was Yaakov? A poor shepherd. And you? Rich and influential. Had you related to Yaakov with fitting sympathy and with faithful kindness, so many sufferings would not have passed over him. You were in the time of Moshe and were counted among Pharaoh's advisers. Did you lift a finger when Pharaoh decreed the decree 'every son that is born you shall cast into the river' (Shemot 1:22), when the taskmasters worked your brothers with rigour? You were silent then and did not protest, because you feared to identify with the wretched slaves. To drop them a coin, yes; but to plead their cause in public, no. You were afraid lest they accuse you of dual loyalty. You were active in the generation of Ezra and Neḥemya, of those who came up from Babylonia. You, Iyov, with your wealth and your influence, could have hastened the process of settling the Land and building the Temple. However, your ear was blocked and did not take in the historic cry of the nation. You did not go out in a storm of protest against the Sanballats, the Samaritans and the other haters of Israel, who wanted to destroy the settlement and extinguish the last spark of hope of the people of God. What did you do when those who came up from the exile cried from the depths of suffering and despair (Neḥemya 4:4): 'The strength of the bearers of burdens is failing, and there is much rubbish, and we are not able to build the wall'? You sat with folded arms! You did not share in the suffering of those fighting for Judaism, the Land of Israel and the redemption; you never brought a single sacrifice for their sake. Only for your own welfare and good did you care all your days, and only for yourself did you pray and offer burnt offerings… Did you ever raise a supplication on behalf of a stranger out of sharing in his pain? No!…" Through the sufferings Iyov will be able to understand his shortcoming and to repair himself.

sections.title_en: How Far the Obligation of Rebuke Extends
sections.body_en:
How many times must one rebuke? The Sages said (Bava Metzia 31a): "'Rebuke': even a hundred times is implied." And this is on condition that there is a chance that the rebuke will be accepted; but if there is no chance at all that the rebuke will be accepted, then the mitzva is to rebuke once, and beyond this one should not rebuke. And as the Sages said (Yevamot 65b): "Just as it is a mitzva for a person to say something that will be heeded, so it is a mitzva for a person not to say something that will not be heeded" (Rema OḤ 608:2; MB 9).

And how is the protest made? The Amora'im disagreed about this. According to Rav, the one who rebukes must rebuke the sinner with such force that the sinner will want to strike him. According to Shmuel, the rebuke must be sharp, but not to the point of striking, rather until the sinner wants to curse him. And according to Rabbi Yoḥanan, the rebuke must be until the sinner reprimands the one who rebukes and tells him severely that he does not want to hear him any more (Arakhin 16b).

The Rishonim disagreed about whose view is the halakha. According to the Semag, the halakha follows R. Yoḥanan, that the rebuke is until reprimand; but the Rambam ruled that the rebuke is until striking. And so he wrote (Laws of Character Traits 6:7): "And so one is always obligated to rebuke until the sinner strikes him and says to him: I will not listen. And whoever is able to protest and does not protest is held responsible for the sin of all those against whom he could have protested."2

As we have learned, when there is a chance that the rebuke will be accepted, one must continue to rebuke up to a hundred times and more, and according to the Rambam until the sinner wants to strike him. But there is no need that it actually reach blows. And when there is no chance that the rebuke will be accepted, one should rebuke once only.

Also when it concerns a public sin, as in a situation in which the government plots to destroy settlements and to oppress their inhabitants, one must protest against it. And as long as there is a chance that the protest will help, one must rebuke and rebuke again until the policemen strike the demonstrators (below, Rav Goren's responsa, siman 1, 13, and siman 4).

Seemingly one should ask: what is the benefit of protest to the point of striking, and especially when there is almost no chance that the protest will help? But one must know that protest has two roles. The first is to try to persuade the sinner to return from his sin. But even when it is clear that the protest will not dissuade him from the sin, there is still a mitzva to rebuke, so that it will be clear to all that the sin is very severe. And why must the protest be sharp, to the point of striking? Because if it is not said sharply, everyone will think the matter is not so severe. And so too it is accepted that people demonstrate with great force when their property or honour is about to be harmed, and no less than this must they demonstrate and protest when there is a plot to harm sacred values.

notes_en.en: When a person rebukes his fellow on a private matter, he should rebuke until reprimand or cursing or striking on condition that the person who sins agrees in principle that one must keep the Torah and the mitzvot, but in this matter his inclination overcame him, and therefore there is a chance that if the rebuke is said again and again decisively it will be accepted. A further condition is that it is clear that even if the rebuke is sharp, afterwards they will return to being friends, since it is clear that it was said out of love and friendship. For if not, his loss is greater than his gain, because if they come to hatred between them through this, they will come to the transgression of "You shall not hate your brother in your heart" (Vayikra 19:17).

sections.body_en:
Throughout the generations, especially in exile, Jews were many times taken captive or kidnapped, and great sums of money were demanded for their redemption. The Sages of Israel addressed this painful subject, and set fundamental rules regarding the very status of the mitzva of redeeming captives, and regarding the price that may be paid for their redemption.

The Sages said that it is a great mitzva to redeem captives, and one should donate money for it, and it takes precedence in importance over all the various kinds of tzedaka, because the captive suffers from hunger, thirst and lack of clothing, and in addition his life is in danger (Bava Batra 8b). Therefore one should not spare efforts in order to save captives (Rambam and SA YD 252:1).

However, the Sages set a halakha that it is forbidden to pay an exorbitant price for redeeming captives, as explained in the Mishna (Gittin 45a): "One does not redeem captives for more than their value, for the sake of tikkun olam (the good order of the world)." The main reason for this enactment, as explained in the Talmud, is so as not to create an incentive for robbers to seize more and more captives of ours, after they know that we are ready to pay any price for them. Indeed, in the Talmud a further reason for the enactment is mentioned: so as not to press the public to donate a great deal of money beyond its strength. However, the view of most Rishonim, namely the Rif, the Rambam, the Rosh and the Tur, is that the main reason for the enactment is so as not to encourage the robbers to seize Jews; and so it is ruled in the Shulḥan Arukh (YD 252:4).

And so it is told about one of the great ones of Israel, Rabbi Meir of Rothenburg (4975-5053; 1215-1293), who was taken captive, because the wicked Emperor Rudolf wanted to fill his empty treasury and demanded an enormous sum for his redemption. The Maharam was put in prison in Ensisheim in Alsace, and his many students wanted to collect the money for his redemption, because according to halakha too, if it concerns a Torah scholar who is the great one of the generation, it is permitted to pay any sum in the world for his redemption. But the Maharam instructed them not to redeem him, because he understood that if they paid so enormous a sum for redeeming his life, the haters of Israel would continue to seize more rabbis and demand huge sums for them. And so Maharam of Rothenburg remained in prison for seven years, until the day of his death. With his greatness of soul and his great devotion for the sake of the community, Maharam of Rothenburg sealed the breach, and saved the great ones of Israel who came after him from captivity, and the masses of Israel from great expenses that might have created economic collapse in the communities.

Indeed, all that one should not pay an exorbitant sum for redemption applies specifically when the public must pay the redemption money. But a rich man who was kidnapped and wishes to redeem himself with his own property may pay any sum he wishes for his redemption. For no danger to the public as a whole is foreseen from this; rather the concern is lest the robbers seize him again after they saw that he is ready to pay huge sums, and this calculation is the private matter of that rich man (SA YD 252:4). But he may not redeem the members of his family for more than their value. And regarding his wife, they disagreed.

sections.title_en: Redeeming Captives Who Are in Danger to Life
sections.body_en:
Some hold that when the kidnappers threaten the life of the kidnapped person and say, "If you do not pay the required sum, we will murder the hostage", it is permitted to pay an excessive sum for him. For the enactment not to pay an excessive ransom applies in an ordinary case of captivity, in which the danger to life is not real and immediate; rather there are many chances that the captors will sell him as a slave or keep him with them. But in a situation in which they threaten to kill him, it concerns actual danger to life, which overrides all the mitzvot of the Torah, and the rabbinic enactment too is void, and one must do everything to redeem him.

By contrast, many poskim, among them the Ramban, hold that even in a case where the kidnappers threaten the captive's life, one should not give in, and it is forbidden to pay an excessive payment. For if they give in, they will create an incentive to seize more captives of ours and even to threaten their lives. Therefore, out of general concern for the welfare of the public, and for the danger to life awaiting captives in the future, it is forbidden to give in to them.

In practice this question was not decided, and the great poskim of the Aḥaronim too disagreed about it (Pitḥei Teshuva YD 252:4).

sections.title_en: Should One Give In to Terrorists' Extortion to Save a Hostage?
sections.body_en:
Question: During the existence of the State there have been cases in which terrorists kidnapped civilians or soldiers and threatened that if we do not release many terrorists from our prisons, they will murder the hostages in their hands. The question is whether according to halakha one must respond to their demand and release many terrorists in order to save the life of a Jew, or whether one should not respond to their extortion.

Answer: In the previous halakhot we learned that as a general rule it is forbidden to give in to the extortion of kidnappers, and when the captive is in tangible danger to life, the poskim disagreed. But all this is said specifically about ordinary criminals, whose whole desire is to make money. But when it concerns a situation of continuous war between us and the terrorists, it is forbidden to give in to any extortion on their part. For if we give in, our enemies will see this as a clear sign of weakness, their morale will rise, and they will continue with greater energy to harm us. And likewise it is known that after every such "success", more terrorists join their ranks. In addition, those who go out to harm us will not fear for their future, because they will rely on the fact that even if they are caught, they will soon be released from the Israeli prison through a release deal. Further, there is a reasonable concern that at least some of the terrorists who are released from prison will return and harm Jews. Therefore, despite the pain in the matter, one should not give in to extortion and pay for the hostage more than is accepted in such cases, that is, a person for a person.

The rule is that in time of war one does not give in to any dictate of the enemy, and if they seized even one captive of ours, one goes out to war for him to save him. For we find in the Torah (Bamidbar 21:1): "And the Canaanite, the king of Arad, who dwelt in the Negev, heard that Israel came by the way of Atharim, and he fought against Israel and took some of them captive." And the Sages said (as brought in Rashi) that they seized only one maidservant from Israel. And to save her, they did not open negotiations, but went out against them to war. And so David did when the Amalekites raided Tziklag and took the women captive: he did not negotiate with them, but fought them and saved the captives (I Shmuel 30). And even if the enemies came to seize only straw and stubble, one goes out against them to war, because if we give in to them in a small matter, they will continue to fight us more and more (Eruvin 45a).

All this is said regarding terrorists and enemies who continue their war. But when it concerns a war that has ended, it is permitted to exchange all the captives in our hands for the captives in their hands, although we hold many more captives. For this is the accepted custom in ceasefire agreements, that all the captives are returned, and this is not considered more than their value, and therefore there is no concern that returning the captives will cause the war to continue. Presumably the considerations for opening a new war will be based on other considerations.3

notes_en.en: So wrote Rav Klav zt"l in Teḥumin 4, 108. However, see Ḥavat Binyamin by Rav Yisraeli 1:16, and in Assia vol. 7 p. 8, who holds that there is permission to exchange one captive of ours for many captives, on the basis of the reasoning that a person is permitted to redeem himself even at an exorbitant price. And in his view every soldier who enlists in the army has, as it were, insured himself against captivity, that they will redeem him at any price. And therefore he permitted the IDF to decide whether to redeem him and at what price. However, in practice we have already seen that one cannot always rely on the judgement of the IDF commanders, some of whom tend to change their position according to political benefit. And it is clear that the prisoner exchanges carried out until now raised the morale of the terrorists, and even among the terrorists who were released, many continued to engage in terror, until the number of those killed by them was greater than the number of our captives who were released. Therefore the view of the rabbis today is that any prisoner exchange at an exorbitant price is forbidden. And likewise the words of Rav Ortner in Teḥumin 13 p. 262, that there is no certainty that the released terrorists will continue in terror, were proven incorrect. Therefore, as long as the struggle continues, there is no permission to exchange captives at an exorbitant price. And so is the view of other rabbis in Judea, Samaria and Gaza. And Rav Goren, in 'Torat Ha-Medina' pp. 424-436, agrees that it is forbidden to give in to the extortion of terrorists; but regarding soldiers who fell captive while carrying out their mission, he wrote that it may be that an absolute obligation rests on the State to redeem them at any price, without taking into account the harm this may cause to security and to the State. And he concludes that it is obligatory to set a death penalty for terrorists, for otherwise there will be no deterrence towards them, since they will rely on being released in a prisoner exchange deal. And Rav Yisraeli too, in Ḥavat Binyamin 17, permitted endangering soldiers so as not to carry out prisoner exchanges when the exchange involves surrender and humiliation of the honour of Israel.

sections.title_en: Is There a Mitzva to Save a Terrorist?
sections.body_en:
Question: Years ago there was a case in which a terrorist tried to murder a Jewish boy in the centre of Jerusalem. By God's kindness the boy was only lightly wounded. Furious citizens who wanted to take revenge on the terrorist and execute judgement on him began to chase him, and one woman shielded the terrorist with her body, and saved him from blows and perhaps even from death. The question is: is it right to save a terrorist, and did that woman act according to halakha?

Answer: There are two sides to the question: from the aspect of the terrorist's status, whether it is fitting to help him; and from the aspect of saving from danger.

Regarding the status of the terrorist, we learned in the Talmud (Avoda Zara 26b) that the law of the great wicked is "one lowers them and does not raise them up". That is, when possible, one makes efforts to bring about their death, and certainly one does not save them (Rambam, Laws of the Murderer 5:10; SA ḤM 425:5). A terrorist who comes to murder Jews in the middle of the street certainly enters this level of wickedness, and at the very least one must refrain from helping him and saving him. Indeed, according to the law set on the basis of international conventions, it is forbidden to kill a terrorist from whom no danger is any longer foreseen, and the law obligates, as we have learned (above in chapter 6). Therefore anyone who is in a state role, as a policeman or a soldier, must act according to the instructions of the law and save the terrorist. And even on Shabbat one must treat enemy wounded according to the international conventions (and see Ḥatam Sofer YD 131; Igrot Moshe 4:79; Melumdei Milḥama 43). But a citizen who is not in a role that obligates him to save the terrorist is not obligated by law to help the terrorist and save him. Therefore it was not right according to halakha to save the terrorist, for it is a settled halakha that "one does not raise up", that is, one does not save such a wicked man. And only when the aim is to uphold the law and to save the citizens from transgressing the law and being punished for it is there virtue in stopping them. But it is not fitting to boast of the very saving of the terrorist.

From the aspect of the danger, that woman did not act according to halakha. For it is clear that as long as danger is foreseen from the terrorist, even a slight doubt of danger, it is a mitzva for every person to save the people who are there by harming the terrorist. For the terrorist has the law of a 'rodef' (pursuer), according to which, whenever it is possible to stop the pursuer by harming one of his limbs, that is preferable. But if there is a concern that even harming one of his limbs will not prevent the danger, or that the attempt to aim precisely and harm one limb will cause a delay in stopping the terrorist and risk to the life of one of the people there, one must kill the pursuing terrorist in order to save the pursued (SA ḤM 425:1). And since it concerns a wicked terrorist, both in terms of his personal status and in terms of his murderous intention, whenever there is a shadow of a doubt of danger, it is a mitzva to kill him in order to prevent the danger. And since in practice they had not yet completely overpowered the terrorist, that woman was forbidden to endanger herself and the others. And in these matters one must be stringent, for there were cases in which they thought they had already overpowered the terrorist and he continued to murder.

sections.title_en: Responsibility for Improving the Condition of All People
sections.body_en:
Not only towards the members of our people do we have responsibility, but towards all people. Indeed, there is an order, and in all matters of tzedaka and kindness one must give precedence to Israel over a gentile; but the complete vision is to do good to all people, and as long as there is pain and suffering in the world, the redemption has not yet come.

And so we learn from Avraham our father, who loved all people and desired to do them good in every respect, and therefore he greatly desired to welcome guests, and he would take trouble over them to give them food and drink and to teach them faith, in order to do them good spiritually and materially.

The Sages said (Bereshit Rabba 50:4) that those angels who came to Avraham our father at the time when he was ill from the brit mila appeared in his eyes as idol worshippers who bow down to the dust of their feet; nevertheless he ran towards them, brought them into his house, and slaughtered for them a calf, tender and good.

Indeed, it is forbidden to forgive idol worshippers and other sinners their sins, and therefore it is forbidden to do kindness with the wicked. But when it is possible to bring them back in repentance and draw them close to the true faith, it is a mitzva to do so, because our basic attitude towards all the gentiles must be one of love. And as our master Rav Kook zt"l wrote: "The love of creatures must be alive in the heart and the soul, the love of all humanity especially, and the love of all the peoples, desire for their elevation and their spiritual and material revival; and the hatred must be only of the wickedness and the filth in the world. It is impossible at all to reach the elevation of spirit of 'Give thanks to the Lord, call upon His name, make known His deeds among the peoples' without inner love, from the depths of heart and soul, to do good to all the peoples, to improve their possessions (their material condition), and to bring happiness to their lives" (to make them happy in their lives). And our master the Rav added that this quality of love and responsibility towards all the peoples prepares us for the spirit of the King Messiah (Middot Ha-Re'aya, Ahava 5).
